I walked to Lodhi Gardens at dawn, seeking the silence of stone, but found only dust and the creaking machinery of the state. Mr. Malhotra, retired after thirty-four years of service, stood before the tombs and offered me the only honest critique I have received in this city: the state does not move; it waits, and one must push it. He speaks of files and decisions; I speak of the Ethical Idea. We are both right, which is the most uncomfortable position for a philosopher. The body, however, demands its due. The sambar, kept warm by Ramesh’s rigid fidelity to the clock, became a ghost haunting my hunger for seven hours. I ate idli at nine, a white cake of order, and roasted corn at two, a humble concession to the tyrant heat. By evening, the hunger had become a philosophical problem. I left the house, walked to Khan Market, and bought a bandhgala, paying the balance in rupees and keeping my Berlin frock coat, a relic of a world that has passed. Masterji’s advice is blunt: the cloth must breathe, not choke. I bought a samosa and chai, small acts of sustenance in a city that consumes its citizens. We are all waiting for the light to fail, for the dialectic to resolve in the dark. The owl spreads its wings only at dusk, and today, the dusk was hot, dusty, and full of creaking machinery.

Shri Hegde, the intended recipient, has agreed to meet me on Monday to settle the matter. He brings the allotment papers; I bring the house. We shall let the record speak.

I walk in Lodhi Garden, where the dust is thick but the light is clear. I meet Mrs. Kapoor, a retired teacher who walks the same path every evening to keep her head clear of clutter. She corrected my philosophical tendency to call her routine 'peace.' It is not peace, she said; it is discipline. I accept her correction. It is sharper than my labels.

The air is clear in the mornings, but the heat rises by noon. I eat chhole and roti, and I walk until the body demands rest.

I have bought a new notebook, as my notes are outgrowing the paper I carry. The next week will be spent waiting for Hegde, reading my own *Phenomenology* by the window, and watching the sun set over the Tughlak Road. I will look for the way the error transforms into a right, or whether it remains merely a residue.

G. W. F. Hegel
